# Find, flag and extract {#sec-uc-extract}



Free-text fields hide structured values -- a postcode at the end of an
address, an amount in a description, a drug name in a case note. This
chapter is about getting them out: flagging records that mention any of a
long list of terms, tolerating misspellings, and extracting fields and
numbers in one vectorised pass.

| Task | Function | Instead of |
|---|---|---|
| Does the text mention any of N terms? Which? How often? | `fgrepl_any()`, `fwhich_any()`, `fcount_any()`, `fextract_any()` | `grepl(paste(terms, collapse = "|"), x)` |
| The same, allowing typos | `fagrepl()`, `fagrep()` | `agrepl()`, `agrep()` |
| First or every regex match, or a capture group | `fextract()`, `fextract_all()` | `regmatches()` + `regexpr()`/`gregexpr()` |
| One field of delimited text | `fsplit_field()` | `sapply(strsplit(x, sep), "[", i)` |
| Numbers inside text | `fparse_number()` | `readr::parse_number()`, `as.numeric(gsub(...))` |
| Count matches per string | `fcount()` | `lengths(gregexpr(...))` with `NA` fixes |

## Flag records that mention any of many terms

Keyword lists are long -- medicines, product codes, place names, sanctions
lists -- and the obvious approaches scale badly: one `grepl()` per term
reads the text once per term, and a single alternation of thousands of
terms is slow for a backtracking regex engine. `fgrepl_any()` and its
siblings build an Aho-Corasick automaton from the terms and read each
string once, however many terms there are:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
notes <- c("Pt given paracetamol 500mg and ibuprofen",
           "Reports nausea after AMOXICILLIN course",
           "No medication. Seen by police at home",
           "Advised to stop taking aspirin; started warfarin",
           "paracetemol 1g PRN",
           "Discussed diet and exercise")
drugs <- c("paracetamol", "ibuprofen", "amoxicillin", "aspirin", "warfarin",
           "ice", "codeine")

data.frame(
    any   = fgrepl_any(drugs, notes, ignore.case = TRUE),
    first = drugs[fwhich_any(drugs, notes, ignore.case = TRUE)],
    count = fcount_any(drugs, notes, ignore.case = TRUE)
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    any       first count
1  TRUE paracetamol     2
2  TRUE amoxicillin     1
3  TRUE         ice     1
4  TRUE     aspirin     2
5 FALSE        <NA>     0
6 FALSE        <NA>     0
```


:::
:::


`fwhich_any()` reports the *first term in the list* that occurs, so the
order of `terms` is a priority order -- put the most specific or most
serious terms first. `fextract_any(all = TRUE)` lists every occurrence.

Two things stand out. The terms are matched as substrings, so `"ice"` (the
street name for methamphetamine) is found inside `"police"`. Pad both sides
with spaces to match whole words only:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
as_words <- function(s) paste0(" ", fsquish(fgsub("[^[:alnum:]]+", " ", s)), " ")
fextract_any(paste0(" ", drugs, " "), as_words(notes), all = TRUE,
             ignore.case = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] " paracetamol " " ibuprofen "  

[[2]]
[1] " AMOXICILLIN "

[[3]]
character(0)

[[4]]
[1] " aspirin "  " warfarin "

[[5]]
character(0)

[[6]]
character(0)
```


:::
:::


And `"paracetemol"` is misspelled, so no exact method finds it -- that is
the next section.

The speed difference is large even for a modest list. Here are 100,000
notes against 2,007 terms:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2)
n <- 1e5
vocab <- c(drugs, "patient", "reviewed", "today", "pain", "mg", "daily",
           "home", "police", "nurse")
big <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(vocab, 8, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")
terms <- c(drugs, vapply(1:2000, function(i) paste(sample(letters, 8, TRUE), collapse = ""), ""))

system.time(hit_fast <- fgrepl_any(terms, big))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   user  system elapsed 
   0.00    0.00    0.02 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
system.time(hit_base <- grepl(paste(terms, collapse = "|"), big))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   user  system elapsed 
  20.06    0.43   20.53 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
identical(hit_fast, hit_base)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


## Allow for typos

`fagrepl()` is `agrepl()` -- the same arguments and the same results --
computed with Myers' bit-parallel algorithm on every core. It finds the
pattern anywhere in each string within `max.distance` edits:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fagrepl("paracetamol", notes, max.distance = 2, ignore.case = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
identical(fagrepl("paracetamol", notes, max.distance = 2, ignore.case = TRUE),
          agrepl("paracetamol", notes, max.distance = 2, ignore.case = TRUE))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


For a list of terms, call it once per term; it is fast enough that a few
hundred terms over a million notes is practical. When the question is
"which dictionary entry is this *whole* value closest to", use
`fuzzy_within()` instead (@sec-uc-link).

## Extract values with regular expressions

`fextract()` returns the first match per string, or one capture group of
it; `fextract_all()` returns every match. Here are the state and postcode
at the end of an Australian address:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
addr <- c("12 Smith St, Brisbane QLD 4000", "Unit 3, 45 North Rd, Darwin NT 0800",
          "PO Box 99, Hobart TAS 7001", "No postcode here")
data.frame(
    state    = fextract("\\b(NSW|QLD|VIC|SA|WA|TAS|NT|ACT)\\s+[0-9]{4}$", addr, group = 1),
    postcode = fextract("\\b(NSW|QLD|VIC|SA|WA|TAS|NT|ACT)\\s+([0-9]{4})$", addr, group = 2)
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  state postcode
1   QLD     4000
2    NT     0800
3   TAS     7001
4  <NA>     <NA>
```


:::
:::


And every phone number or email address in a message:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
msg <- c("Call 0412 345 678 or 07 3123 4567", "email a.b@x.com, c@y.org", "nothing")
fextract_all("0[0-9][0-9 ]{7,11}[0-9]", msg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] "0412 345 678" "07 3123 4567"

[[2]]
character(0)

[[3]]
character(0)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fextract_all("[[:alnum:]._]+@[[:alnum:].]+\\.[a-z]+", msg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
character(0)

[[2]]
[1] "a.b@x.com" "c@y.org"  

[[3]]
character(0)
```


:::
:::


Patterns follow the same rules as `fgrepl()`: base R's extended regular
expressions by default, PCRE with `perl = TRUE`, literal text with
`fixed = TRUE`. Strings with no match give `NA` (or `character(0)` from
`fextract_all()`), so the result lines up with the input row for row.

## Split delimited fields

`fsplit_field()` returns one field of delimited text without building the
list that `strsplit()` would, which matters when you only want one or two
fields of millions of rows:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
full <- c("SMITH, John Paul", "O'BRIEN, Mary", "NGUYEN,Van  Anh", "MADONNA")
data.frame(full,
           surname = fsplit_field(full, ",", 1, fixed = TRUE),
           given   = fsquish(fsplit_field(full, ",", 2, fixed = TRUE)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
              full surname     given
1 SMITH, John Paul   SMITH John Paul
2    O'BRIEN, Mary O'BRIEN      Mary
3  NGUYEN,Van  Anh  NGUYEN   Van Anh
4          MADONNA MADONNA      <NA>
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
codes <- c("QLD|4000|BRISBANE", "NSW|2000|SYDNEY|CBD", "VIC||MELBOURNE")
data.frame(state    = fsplit_field(codes, "|", 1, fixed = TRUE),
           postcode = fsplit_field(codes, "|", 2, fixed = TRUE),
           last     = fsplit_field(codes, "|", -1, fixed = TRUE))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  state postcode      last
1   QLD     4000  BRISBANE
2   NSW     2000       CBD
3   VIC          MELBOURNE
```


:::
:::


Every field counts, including empty ones (`"VIC||MELBOURNE"` has an empty
postcode), and negative positions count from the end.

## Numbers inside text

Amounts typed into free-text or spreadsheet columns come with currency
symbols, thousands separators, units and labels. `fparse_number()` finds
the first number in each string and ignores the rest:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prices <- c("$1,234.50", "AUD 99", "12.5%", "approx. 3,000 kg", "-$45.10",
            "(1,200)", "N/A", "Free")
data.frame(prices,
           fparse_number = fparse_number(prices),
           readr = suppressWarnings(readr::parse_number(prices)),
           gsub  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.-]", "", prices))))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
            prices fparse_number  readr   gsub
1        $1,234.50        1234.5 1234.5 1234.5
2           AUD 99          99.0   99.0   99.0
3            12.5%          12.5   12.5   12.5
4 approx. 3,000 kg        3000.0     NA    0.3
5          -$45.10         -45.1     NA  -45.1
6          (1,200)        1200.0 1200.0 1200.0
7              N/A            NA     NA     NA
8             Free            NA     NA     NA
```


:::
:::


The common shortcut of deleting everything but digits fails as soon as the
text contains another full stop (`"approx."` becomes `0.3`).
`readr::parse_number()` returns `NA` for that case and for a minus sign in
front of a currency symbol, and (in our tests) rounds about a quarter of
two-decimal amounts to a neighbouring double; `fparse_number()` returns
exactly what `as.numeric()` gives for the number it finds. Accounting-style negatives such as
`"(1,200)"` are read as positive by both, so test for the parentheses
separately if your data uses them. Other conventions are one argument
away:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fparse_number(c("1.234,50 \u20ac", "12,5 %", "1 234 567,89"),
              decimal_mark = ",", grouping_mark = c(".", " "))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]    1234.5      12.5 1234567.9
```


:::
:::


## Count things per record

`fcount()` counts matches per string, which turns data-quality rules into
one vectorised call each -- digits in a name field, or the number of words:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
names <- c("JOHN SMITH", "KYLE 2", "UNKNOWN 0000", "MARY-JANE O'NEIL")
data.frame(names, digits = fcount("[0-9]", names), words = fcount("[^ ]+", names))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             names digits words
1       JOHN SMITH      0     2
2           KYLE 2      1     2
3     UNKNOWN 0000      4     2
4 MARY-JANE O'NEIL      0     2
```


:::
:::


@sec-uc-profile builds on this to profile whole columns.
